reason: After a worker-start timeout, auto-admission kept the prepared worker's runtime ID until an attach fully succeeded and blocked the project until the host or memory-policy revision changed, with no time-based retry. An attach that timed out after the grant committed left the ID behind; once that worker retired, the next readmission re-attached the dead process (connection refused) and the project stayed without a worker until Core restarted. A prepared worker is now forgotten only on SQL evidence (owns the project, not attachable, or serves another project), failed admissions retry with a bounded backoff (and at once on a revision change) without starving other projects, diagnostics name the project and attempt and flag a persistent failure, and the attach wait tolerates a slow status read within its bound. Rebased onto #1028 (queued project commands admit a worker) and #1032 (no claim onto a worker an aborted shutdown closed): the demand query keeps #1028's queued-work demand, archived-with-work admission and retirement-hold exclusion, and adds this change's backoff exclusion. Selection covers the stale-worker readmission, backoff without a revision change, the persistent-failure diagnostic, the slow status read, #1028's chatless edit/archived delete admission, retirement and ingress-wait cases and its retirement contract tests, #1032's aborted-shutdown claim and retirement cases, and the existing admission, readmission, held-project, auto-recovery and API worker cases.
exclusions: No UI, native or frontend code changed, so no frontend, native or Playwright tests. The real-Core stall reproduction (SIGSTOP of a starting worker, retire, new chat) was run by hand on scratch supervisor Cores on main and on this change (see the PR). PostgreSQL parametrizations are collected but skip in CI; they pass locally on PostgreSQL 16. No live or staging Core mutation, database backup, or deployment.
